newsitem.title: CANADA: De Gaulle statue sparks controversy in Quebec.
newsitem.headline: De Gaulle statue sparks controversy in Quebec.

text.p: Charles de Gaulle returned to haunt Canadian politics on Wednesday when Quebec's capital erected a monument to the French leader 30 years after his explosive speech in support of the province's independence.

Amid cheers and protests, the city unveiled a bronze statue of the general on the Plains of Abraham, a park overlooking the St. Lawrence River where British troops defeated the French in 1759 for control of Canada.

Quebec City Mayor Jean-Paul L'Allier, who supports the separation of the French-speaking province from Canada, said the 8.5-foot (2.6-m) statue was recognition of de Gaulle's role in forging close relations between Quebec and France.
"Vive le Quebec libre (Long live a free Quebec)," de Gaulle proclaimed to an ecstatic crowd from the balcony of Montreal's city hall in 1967. The French president's words sparked a diplomatic storm.
"There are people who want separatists to go away, but we will never go away," the mayor said of the statue's opponents.
Pierre Messmer, a defense minister under de Gaulle, drew loud cheers from a crowd of several hundred people attending the statue's unveiling when he recalled de Gaulle's words.
"Four simple and powerful words that reaffirm a universal and indisputable principle -- the inalienable right of people to decide their own future," Messmer said.
De Gaulle's speech boosted separatist sentiments in Quebec just as Canada was celebrating its centennial.

Lester Pearson, Canada's prime minister at the time, issued an official rebuke, saying all Canadians were free people and did not need to be liberated. De Gaulle left Canada without visiting Ottawa as planned.
The monument was paid for by Quebec's separatist Parti Quebecois government. It annoyed English Canadians who oppose Quebec separation, including a group of Canadian war veterans.

"Eighty thousand Canadians died during World War to liberate France, while de Gaulle was sitting comfortably in London, but it was he who entered Paris as a liberator," Canadian Second World War veteran Pierre Roy told reporters.
Messmer was accompanied at the unveiling ceremony by Philippe Sequin, president of the French opposition party, Rassemblement pour la Republique (RPR).
The Canadian government lamented the divisive event.
"It is too bad that a person as great as he has been in this century is celebrated in a way that divides Quebeckers," Stephane Dion, the federal minister responsible for Quebec, said in Ottawa.
"One way to avoid it would have been to celebrate all his trips to Quebec, notably his first one where he said Canada was a courageous and beloved country," Dion said.
During the Quebec City ceremony, protesters waved the Canadian flag and sang Canada's national anthem. One woman was arrested when she tried to drape the Canadian flag around the statue.
Some protesters shouted "Vive la Bretagne libre" (Long live a free Brittany) and "Vive la Corse libre" (Long live a free Corsica).
"It means nothing to me. I would have preferred a statue of Queen Elizabeth," said Marguerite Tardivel.
Supporters cheered, waved Quebec's fleur-de-lis flag or quietly watched the ceremony. Another rally commemorating de Gaulle's speech was planned for Thursday night at Montreal's City Hall.
"De Gaulle gave Quebec hope. The statue will bring tourists," said Delphine-Anne Rousseau, who lives near the monument.
